notes: 25 independently written AQA-style Chemistry standalone questions plus seven original multipart subparts; not past-paper reproductions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: A sample contains one halide. Acidified silver nitrate gives a cream precipitate insoluble in dilute ammonia but soluble in concentrated ammonia. Identify the halide, give the net ionic equation and explain why nitric acid is used.
markPoints: The ion is Br⁻, giving pale cream AgBr.
Ag⁺(aq)+Br⁻(aq)→AgBr(s).
AgBr is insoluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia.
Nitric acid removes carbonate interference without introducing chloride ions.
questions.modelAnswer: The ion is Br⁻, giving pale cream AgBr. Ag⁺(aq)+Br⁻(aq)→AgBr(s). AgBr is insoluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia. Nitric acid removes carbonate interference without introducing chloride ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Predict the molecular shapes and approximate bond angles of NH3 and BF3 using electron-pair repulsion. Explain why they differ despite both having three bonded atoms.
markPoints: NH3 has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, giving trigonal pyramidal shape.
H–N–H angle is about 107° because lone pair repulsion compresses the angle.
BF3 has three bonding regions and no lone pair, giving trigonal planar shape.
F–B–F angle is 120° because bonding regions repel symmetrically.
questions.modelAnswer: NH3 has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, giving trigonal pyramidal shape. H–N–H angle is about 107° because lone pair repulsion compresses the angle. BF3 has three bonding regions and no lone pair, giving trigonal planar shape. F–B–F angle is 120° because bonding regions repel symmetrically.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Compare the major products of reacting 2-bromobutane with warm aqueous hydroxide and with hot ethanolic hydroxide. Explain the different organic reaction types.
markPoints: Aqueous OH⁻ favours nucleophilic substitution yielding butan-2-ol.
OH⁻ replaces the bromine, which leaves as bromide.
Hot ethanolic OH⁻ favours elimination producing a mixture of butenes.
A base abstracts H from a neighbouring carbon as the halogen leaves, creating C=C.
questions.modelAnswer: Aqueous OH⁻ favours nucleophilic substitution yielding butan-2-ol. OH⁻ replaces the bromine, which leaves as bromide. Hot ethanolic OH⁻ favours elimination producing a mixture of butenes. A base abstracts H from a neighbouring carbon as the halogen leaves, creating C=C.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Write the balanced complete combustion equation for propane and explain the different hazards of its incomplete combustion in limited oxygen.
markPoints: Adequate oxygen enables complete oxidation of carbon to CO2.
Insufficient oxygen may produce poisonous carbon monoxide.
Incomplete burning may also produce particulate solid carbon or soot.
questions.modelAnswer: C3H8+5O2→3CO2+4H2O. Adequate oxygen enables complete oxidation of carbon to CO2. Insufficient oxygen may produce poisonous carbon monoxide. Incomplete burning may also produce particulate solid carbon or soot.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Cyclohexene reacts with bromine water. State the observation, product formula and explain the electrophilic-addition process, including what happens to the C=C bond.
markPoints: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless.
The product 1,2-dibromocyclohexane has formula C6H10Br2.
The alkene π electrons polarise Br2 and react with an electrophilic bromine atom.
Bromide subsequently attacks the intermediate, producing a saturated dibromo compound.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless. The product 1,2-dibromocyclohexane has formula C6H10Br2. The alkene π electrons polarise Br2 and react with an electrophilic bromine atom. Bromide subsequently attacks the intermediate, producing a saturated dibromo compound.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Oxidation of propan-1-ol with acidified dichromate is carried out with immediate distillation in one experiment and prolonged reflux with excess oxidant in another. Compare products and observations.
markPoints: Distillation helps isolate propanal before further oxidation.
Excess oxidant under reflux converts the primary alcohol to propanoic acid.
Dichromate(VI) is reduced, with solution changing orange to green.
Removing propanal avoids further oxidation, while reflux retains it to react again.
questions.modelAnswer: Distillation helps isolate propanal before further oxidation. Excess oxidant under reflux converts the primary alcohol to propanoic acid. Dichromate(VI) is reduced, with solution changing orange to green. Removing propanal avoids further oxidation, while reflux retains it to react again.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Ethanol and dimethyl ether both have formula C2H6O but very different boiling temperatures. Explain why ethanol boils higher, naming relevant intermolecular forces.
markPoints: Both substances experience London forces and permanent dipole interactions.
Ethanol molecules also form intermolecular hydrogen bonds via O–H.
Dimethyl ether lacks an O–H bond, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
More energy is needed to overcome ethanol's stronger intermolecular attractions.
questions.modelAnswer: Both substances experience London forces and permanent dipole interactions. Ethanol molecules also form intermolecular hydrogen bonds via O–H. Dimethyl ether lacks an O–H bond, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. More energy is needed to overcome ethanol's stronger intermolecular attractions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: The time for a disappearing cross is 125 s at one reactant concentration and 50.0 s when that concentration is doubled. Calculate the factor increase in 1/time and explain a limitation of using this observation to infer rate order.
markPoints: The initial relative rate is 1/125=0.00800 s⁻¹.
The later relative rate is 1/50.0=0.0200 s⁻¹.
Their ratio is 2.50.
The endpoint timing is only a proxy for initial rate, and more controlled concentration data are needed to determine order reliably.
questions.modelAnswer: The initial relative rate is 1/125=0.00800 s⁻¹. The later relative rate is 1/50.0=0.0200 s⁻¹. Their ratio is 2.50. The endpoint timing is only a proxy for initial rate, and more controlled concentration data are needed to determine order reliably.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Explain why simple distillation is suitable for collecting propanal during the oxidation of propan-1-ol. State the appropriate position of the thermometer bulb and direction of condenser cooling water.
markPoints: Propanal is separated as vapour as soon as it forms, limiting further oxidation.
The thermometer bulb should be level with the side-arm to measure vapour temperature.
Cooling water enters the condenser jacket at the lower connection.
Water exits at the top, keeping the jacket full for effective condensation.
questions.modelAnswer: Propanal is separated as vapour as soon as it forms, limiting further oxidation. The thermometer bulb should be level with the side-arm to measure vapour temperature. Cooling water enters the condenser jacket at the lower connection. Water exits at the top, keeping the jacket full for effective condensation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: An unknown organic liquid forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Explain what each result shows and identify the functional group.
markPoints: A 2,4-DNPH precipitate indicates an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl group.
Tollens' reagent is reduced to metallic silver by an aldehyde.
Taken together these show the compound is an aldehyde.
2,4-DNPH alone cannot distinguish aldehydes from ketones because both react.
questions.modelAnswer: A 2,4-DNPH precipitate indicates an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl group. Tollens' reagent is reduced to metallic silver by an aldehyde. Taken together these show the compound is an aldehyde. 2,4-DNPH alone cannot distinguish aldehydes from ketones because both react.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: State what happens when sodium hydroxide is added to solutions containing Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Explain why one precipitate changes colour after standing in air.
markPoints: Fe²⁺ initially forms green Fe(OH)2.
Fe³⁺ gives brown Fe(OH)3.
The green iron(II) precipitate becomes browner in air.
Oxygen oxidises Fe²⁺ species to Fe³⁺ species.
questions.modelAnswer: Fe²⁺ initially forms green Fe(OH)2. Fe³⁺ gives brown Fe(OH)3. The green iron(II) precipitate becomes browner in air. Oxygen oxidises Fe²⁺ species to Fe³⁺ species.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Explain why benzene reacts with bromine through electrophilic substitution rather than an addition reaction under suitable conditions. Include how the catalyst operates and the importance of delocalisation.
markPoints: Benzene contains a delocalised π electron system around the ring.
FeBr3 or another halogen carrier polarises bromine to create a stronger electrophile.
Substitution restores aromatic delocalisation after H⁺ loss.
An addition product would destroy the stable delocalised aromatic system.
questions.modelAnswer: Benzene contains a delocalised π electron system around the ring. FeBr3 or another halogen carrier polarises bromine to create a stronger electrophile. Substitution restores aromatic delocalisation after H⁺ loss. An addition product would destroy the stable delocalised aromatic system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Compare the acid-base behaviour of sodium oxide and sulfur dioxide with water, using a balanced equation for each and bonding to explain their different properties.
markPoints: Na2O+H2O→2NaOH, producing alkali.
SO2+H2O⇌H2SO3, giving an acidic solution.
Sodium oxide is an ionic oxide and is basic.
SO2 is a covalent acidic oxide that forms acidic species in water.
questions.modelAnswer: Na2O+H2O→2NaOH, producing alkali. SO2+H2O⇌H2SO3, giving an acidic solution. Sodium oxide is an ionic oxide and is basic. SO2 is a covalent acidic oxide that forms acidic species in water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Contrast magnesium and barium in cold water and explain the general Group 2 reactivity trend in terms of electron shielding, atomic radius and ionisation energies.
markPoints: Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water; barium reacts much more readily.
Atomic radius and shielding increase down the group.
Outer electrons feel weaker nuclear attraction and are removed more easily.
First/second ionisation energies decrease and metal reactivity increases.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water; barium reacts much more readily. Atomic radius and shielding increase down the group. Outer electrons feel weaker nuclear attraction and are removed more easily. First/second ionisation energies decrease and metal reactivity increases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: At a particular temperature, Kw is 5.0×10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. Calculate the pH of pure water and explain why water remains neutral at this temperature.
markPoints: In pure water [H⁺]=[OH⁻]=√Kw.
Pure water is neutral because [H⁺]=[OH⁻] even though neutral pH is not always 7.
questions.modelAnswer: In pure water [H⁺]=[OH⁻]=√Kw. [H⁺]=2.24×10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³. pH=−log10(2.24×10⁻⁷)=6.65. Pure water is neutral because [H⁺]=[OH⁻] even though neutral pH is not always 7.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: A liquid has a strong IR absorption around 1715 cm⁻¹ but lacks a broad carboxylic-acid O–H absorption. It gives no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Suggest the most likely carbonyl group and justify each inference.
markPoints: The 1715 cm⁻¹ absorption suggests C=O.
Absence of the broad acid O–H band makes a carboxylic acid less likely.
Negative Tollens' test argues against an aldehyde.
A ketone is the most likely group, subject to further confirmation.
questions.modelAnswer: The 1715 cm⁻¹ absorption suggests C=O. Absence of the broad acid O–H band makes a carboxylic acid less likely. Negative Tollens' test argues against an aldehyde. A ketone is the most likely group, subject to further confirmation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Explain why aqueous copper(II) solutions are coloured and why excess ammonia produces a deeper blue solution, in terms of complexes and ligand exchange.
markPoints: Cu²⁺ exists as hydrated complex ions such as [Cu(H2O)6]²⁺.
Ligands split d orbital energies, enabling visible-light d–d absorption.
Excess ammonia replaces water ligands to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]²⁺.
Changed ligand field changes d-orbital splitting and therefore light absorption.
questions.modelAnswer: Cu²⁺ exists as hydrated complex ions such as [Cu(H2O)6]²⁺. Ligands split d orbital energies, enabling visible-light d–d absorption. Excess ammonia replaces water ligands to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]²⁺. Changed ligand field changes d-orbital splitting and therefore light absorption.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: For A(g)+2B(g)⇌C(g), equilibrium partial pressures are pA=0.40 atm, pB=0.30 atm and pC=0.18 atm. Calculate Kp and explain what happens immediately after adding extra B at constant temperature.
markPoints: Kp=pC/(pA×pB²).
Kp=5.0 atm⁻².
Adding B reduces Qp below Kp, moving equilibrium right while Kp stays constant.
questions.modelAnswer: Kp=pC/(pA×pB²). Substitute 0.18/[0.40×(0.30)²]. Kp=5.0 atm⁻². Adding B reduces Qp below Kp, moving equilibrium right while Kp stays constant.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: A weak monoprotic acid HA has concentration 0.0800 mol dm⁻³ and Ka=1.8×10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Estimate its pH and justify assuming only a small fraction dissociates.
markPoints: Ka≈[H⁺]²/c for low dissociation.
Degree of dissociation ≈1.5%, supporting the approximation.
questions.modelAnswer: Ka≈[H⁺]²/c for low dissociation. [H⁺]≈√(1.8×10⁻⁵×0.0800)=1.20×10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pH=−log10(1.20×10⁻³)=2.92. Degree of dissociation ≈1.5%, supporting the approximation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Explain why the first ionisation energy generally rises across Period 3 but falls from Mg to Al. Refer to nuclear charge, shielding and sub-shell energy.
markPoints: Nuclear charge rises across Period 3.
Shielding is broadly similar because electrons are added to the same main shell.
Atomic radius tends to decrease, raising first ionisation energy generally.
Al's electron is removed from 3p, which is higher in energy than Mg's 3s electron, producing the dip.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge rises across Period 3. Shielding is broadly similar because electrons are added to the same main shell. Atomic radius tends to decrease, raising first ionisation energy generally. Al's electron is removed from 3p, which is higher in energy than Mg's 3s electron, producing the dip.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 21(a)
questions.prompt: The following initial-rate results were obtained at constant temperature (concentrations in mol dm⁻³, rates in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹): experiment 1: [A]=0.10, [B]=0.10, rate=1.20×10⁻⁴; experiment 2: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.10, rate=4.80×10⁻⁴; experiment 3: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.20, rate=9.60×10⁻⁴. (a) Determine the order with respect to A and the order with respect to B. Explain using the experimental comparisons.
markPoints: Doubling [A] at fixed [B] in experiments 1 and 2 increases the rate by a factor of 4.
The reaction is second order with respect to A.
Doubling [B] at fixed [A] in experiments 2 and 3 doubles the rate, so it is first order with respect to B.
questions.modelAnswer: Doubling [A] at fixed [B] in experiments 1 and 2 increases the rate by a factor of 4. The reaction is second order with respect to A. Doubling [B] at fixed [A] in experiments 2 and 3 doubles the rate, so it is first order with respect to B.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 21(b)
questions.prompt: The following initial-rate results were obtained at constant temperature (concentrations in mol dm⁻³, rates in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹): experiment 1: [A]=0.10, [B]=0.10, rate=1.20×10⁻⁴; experiment 2: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.10, rate=4.80×10⁻⁴; experiment 3: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.20, rate=9.60×10⁻⁴. (b) Calculate the rate constant k in rate=k[A]²[B] and give its units.
markPoints: Substitute a complete set of experimental data, for example k=4.80×10⁻⁴/(0.20²×0.10).
Calculate k=0.120.
Give units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitute a complete set of experimental data, for example k=4.80×10⁻⁴/(0.20²×0.10). Calculate k=0.120. Give units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 21(c)
questions.prompt: The following initial-rate results were obtained at constant temperature (concentrations in mol dm⁻³, rates in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹): experiment 1: [A]=0.10, [B]=0.10, rate=1.20×10⁻⁴; experiment 2: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.10, rate=4.80×10⁻⁴; experiment 3: [A]=0.20, [B]=0.20, rate=9.60×10⁻⁴. (c) Use the experiments to calculate the initial rate when [A]=0.150 mol dm⁻³ and [B]=0.300 mol dm⁻³.
markPoints: Use rate=0.120×0.150²×0.300 with the second and first orders established from the data.
Obtain rate=8.10×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Use rate=0.120×0.150²×0.300 with the second and first orders established from the data. Obtain rate=8.10×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 22(a)
questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka=1.80×10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 25 °C. Assume volumes are additive and use pH=pKa+log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]) within the buffer region. (a) Calculate the pH immediately after 12.5 cm³ of NaOH has been added.
markPoints: Original acid amount is 2.50 mmol and 1.25 mmol OH⁻ reacts, leaving 1.25 mmol HA and producing 1.25 mmol A⁻.
Because [A⁻]/[HA]=1, pH=pKa.
questions.modelAnswer: Original acid amount is 2.50 mmol and 1.25 mmol OH⁻ reacts, leaving 1.25 mmol HA and producing 1.25 mmol A⁻. Because [A⁻]/[HA]=1, pH=pKa. pH=−log₁₀(1.80×10⁻⁵)=4.74 or 4.745.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 22(b)
questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka=1.80×10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 25 °C. Assume volumes are additive and use pH=pKa+log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]) within the buffer region. (b) Calculate the pH immediately after 20.0 cm³ of NaOH has been added.
markPoints: Original HA amount is 2.50 mmol; 2.00 mmol OH⁻ reacts, leaving 0.50 mmol HA and producing 2.00 mmol A⁻.
Use [A⁻]/[HA]=2.00/0.50=4.00 in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Original HA amount is 2.50 mmol; 2.00 mmol OH⁻ reacts, leaving 0.50 mmol HA and producing 2.00 mmol A⁻. Use [A⁻]/[HA]=2.00/0.50=4.00 in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. pH=4.7447+log₁₀(4.00)=5.35.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 23(a)
questions.prompt: A hypothetical reaction has ΔH=−75.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS=−150 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, both assumed constant over the temperature range. Use ΔG=ΔH−TΔS and assume feasibility is assessed by the sign of ΔG. (a) Calculate ΔG at 298 K in kJ mol⁻¹ and state whether the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under the stated assumptions.
markPoints: Convert entropy to −0.150 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and substitute ΔG=−75.0−298(−0.150).
ΔG=−30.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
Since ΔG is negative at 298 K, the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert entropy to −0.150 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and substitute ΔG=−75.0−298(−0.150). ΔG=−30.3 kJ mol⁻¹. Since ΔG is negative at 298 K, the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 23(b)
questions.prompt: A hypothetical reaction has ΔH=−75.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS=−150 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, both assumed constant over the temperature range. Use ΔG=ΔH−TΔS and assume feasibility is assessed by the sign of ΔG. (b) Find the temperature at which ΔG=0 and state the temperature range over which ΔG<0.
markPoints: ΔG is negative for T<500 K (positive above 500 K).
questions.modelAnswer: Set −75.0+0.150T=0, giving T=500 K. ΔG is negative for T<500 K (positive above 500 K).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: At a fixed temperature, the gas equilibrium 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) has equilibrium partial pressures of 30.0 kPa for SO₂, 20.0 kPa for O₂ and 40.0 kPa for SO₃. Calculate Kp with its units, then predict and explain the equilibrium shift when the container volume is reduced at constant temperature.
markPoints: Kp = (pSO₃)² / ((pSO₂)² × pO₂).
Substitution gives Kp = 40.0² / (30.0² × 20.0) = 0.0889.
The units are kPa⁻¹ because the overall pressure exponent is −1.
Reducing volume raises pressure and favours SO₃ on the right, which has two gas molecules rather than three.
questions.modelAnswer: Kp = (pSO₃)² / ((pSO₂)² × pO₂). Substitution gives Kp = 40.0² / (30.0² × 20.0) = 0.0889. The units are kPa⁻¹ because the overall pressure exponent is −1. Reducing volume raises pressure and favours SO₃ on the right, which has two gas molecules rather than three.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: The ionic product of water at 40 °C is Kw = 2.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. Calculate the pH of pure water at this temperature and explain why the water is still neutral even though its pH is not 7. Show how you obtain the hydrogen ion concentration.
markPoints: For pure water, [H⁺] = [OH⁻] and Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻].
Therefore [H⁺] = √Kw = √(2.92 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.71 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.
The water remains neutral because [H⁺] equals [OH⁻]; neutrality does not require pH 7 at every temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: For pure water, [H⁺] = [OH⁻] and Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]. Therefore [H⁺] = √Kw = √(2.92 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 1.71 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(1.71 × 10⁻⁷) = 6.77. The water remains neutral because [H⁺] equals [OH⁻]; neutrality does not require pH 7 at every temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: For a reaction at constant temperature, the rate equation is rate = k[A][B]², where k = 0.040 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate the initial rate when [A] = 0.30 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Predict the effect on the rate if [B] is halved while [A] and temperature remain constant, and state what happens to k.
markPoints: Substitute rate = 0.040 × 0.30 × (0.20)².
The initial rate is 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
Halving [B] reduces the rate to one quarter because the reaction is second order in B.
The rate constant k remains unchanged because temperature is constant.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitute rate = 0.040 × 0.30 × (0.20)². The initial rate is 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Halving [B] reduces the rate to one quarter because the reaction is second order in B. The rate constant k remains unchanged because temperature is constant.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: In a theoretical Friedel–Crafts acylation, benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride and AlCl₃ acts as a catalyst. Outline the electrophilic substitution mechanism, identifying the electrophile, the role of benzene electrons, how aromaticity is restored and the organic product.
markPoints: AlCl₃ accepts chloride from CH₃COCl, generating the CH₃CO⁺ acylium electrophile and AlCl₄⁻.
Benzene's delocalised π electrons attack CH₃CO⁺, forming a positively charged intermediate.
AlCl₄⁻ removes a proton from the intermediate, restoring aromaticity and regenerating AlCl₃.
The organic product is phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃, and HCl is also formed.
questions.modelAnswer: AlCl₃ accepts chloride from CH₃COCl, generating the CH₃CO⁺ acylium electrophile and AlCl₄⁻. Benzene's delocalised π electrons attack CH₃CO⁺, forming a positively charged intermediate. AlCl₄⁻ removes a proton from the intermediate, restoring aromaticity and regenerating AlCl₃. The organic product is phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃, and HCl is also formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Independent practice
questions.prompt: Consider the equilibrium [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. Describe the colour, shape and coordination number of the copper complexes, explain why replacing water with chloride changes the coordination number, and predict the effect of increasing chloride concentration.
markPoints: The hexaaquacopper(II) complex is blue, octahedral and has coordination number six.
The tetrachlorocuprate(II) complex is yellow-green, tetrahedral and has coordination number four.
Chloride ions are larger ligands than water molecules, so fewer fit around Cu²⁺.
Adding chloride shifts the equilibrium towards [CuCl₄]²⁻, making the yellow-green complex more abundant.
questions.modelAnswer: The hexaaquacopper(II) complex is blue, octahedral and has coordination number six. The tetrachlorocuprate(II) complex is yellow-green, tetrahedral and has coordination number four. Chloride ions are larger ligands than water molecules, so fewer fit around Cu²⁺. Adding chloride shifts the equilibrium towards [CuCl₄]²⁻, making the yellow-green complex more abundant.
